Nuclear Fallout

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Hope for millions of people living in radioactive waste on the Witwatersrand gold fields - science steps in to bring their health plight to light

Summary:
Hair tells a story, just like the rings on a tree or the circles on a turtle’s shell. Hair keeps everything that is put into the body – medication, drugs…and in a new study commissioned by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, an agency of the World Health Organisation, the hope is that for the first time hair will confirm the story, backed by science, that anecdotes of mental retardation, cancer and kidney disease have hinted at – namely that the uraniferous mine residue in the Witwatersrand Gold Fields can kill. And that urgent intervention is needed to save lives.
In eight mining areas of the West Rand, the WHO has, after decades of tireless campaigning and activism, contracted the Federation for a Sustainable Environment to conduct a ground-breaking study to determine the effects of exposure to radio-active uranium-rich mine waste in the area.
The Witwatersrand has 20 times more uranium dumps than the United States and Canada combined. More than 600 abandoned mines surround Joburg, with much of their waste now piled up high next to an estimated 1,6-million people – most of whom are poor and black and up to now powerless to take the fight in any direction because of a lack of solid science and an abundance of denial both form organized mining and the state.
Mariette Liefferink from the FSE will now collect hair samples form cooperating hair salons near the waste dumps and send it off to three laboratories in three different countries, together with hair samples from salons further away from dumps – like in Alexandra, Randburg, Laudium and Lenasia. The FSE is conducting this research under supervision of the Northern West University.

Further information:
The New Nuclear Backdrop
President Jacob Zuma’s remarks during last week’s SONA on the country’s nuclear future might seem contradictory, but this is not the case, according to the organized nuclear industry.
Zuma actually meant that South Africa’s nuclear build programme would roll out at a pace the country can afford and that the plan was to introduce 9600MW of nuclear energy in the next decade, they insist. Nuke lobbyists have been at pains to contain popular sentiment and to emphasise that the process of nuclear procurement has been extremely open and transparent – vendor parades were well documented within the confidentiality constraints of a competitive bidding process. Government has cancelled an unaffordable tender process in 2009 indicating the commitment to affordability.
Basically, according to the pro-nuclear lobby, South Africa remains committed to 9600MW of Nuclear New Build, but we will do it at a scale and pace the country can afford and nuclear power remains by far the safest option
What the nuclear industry fails to be transparent about is how much the mining of uranium will be upscaled to meet the demand of a new reactor. Whether environmental and health risks would even be considered.
 
Science to the Rescue
There seems to be an epidemic of cancer besetting the mining areas. Neighborhoods like Bekkersdal, sandwiched in between tailings dams and active mines, where virtually everyone in vivacious, energetic Cecilia Mollo’s street has cancer or know of someone who has fought or died of cancer.
Thanks to the efforts of this former traffic official turned cancer activist, there is even more hope that science will bring to light an issue shrouded in mystery and denial from big mines, the uranium industry and even government.
Cecilia lost her mother to melanoma, and her 19-year old sister to leukaemia. More recently she helped her 73-year old father battle prostate cancer. These experiences have opened the door to people taking Cecilia into their confidence about the great taboo of cancer – apart from believing it’s a white person’s disease, the prevalence just is not as high in other communities as it is here, around the mines.
There’s also a wholesale ignorance of the contents of the uranium rich mine dumps in this area where pregnant women even collect the sand from the tailings, make mud and dry it into little cakes that they sell for as little as R5,00 a bag. The soil is bitten off or sucked and apparently satisfies hunger pangs and pregnancy cravings and tastes something like white chocolate. Except for the dire danger inherent in directly ingesting radio-active waste.
Cecilia founded her own NGO to raise the issue, provide support – form getting money for people to get transport to hospitals in Johannesburg or Soweto, Baragwanath – over 60km away, since there are no oncology clinics in the area.
Her own experiences with cancer and her steadfast outreach into the community had helped Cecilia collect anecdotes all over the township, and allowed her to present her preliminary findings both to the powerful Treatment Action Campaign as well as the internationally respected Medecins Sans Frontiers.
The TAC assigned the soft-spoken Tsepho Maboe to help Cecilia conduct a door-to-door mapping of the Bekkersdal community to determine the extent of the prevalence of cancer. In no time Maboe has turned his extensive understanding of HIV and how to care for people into a deepening understanding of cancer.
Once Cecilia and Tsepho have done the mapping, they have the promise from MSF that the research will form the basis of the first epidemiological study of cancer in the West Rand; and the Legal Resources Centre have suggested that the narratives be used as the basis for affidavits for a class action lawsuit.
The people who live in the area we will show are all exposed to the uranium and other highly radioactive elements that come from the tailings dams in the catchment of the Upper Wonderfontein Spruit. In this catchment is the Lancaster Dam and an informal settlement on a nuclear dump that are said to be in the same order of radioactivity as the fall-out zone around Chernobyl.
 
Reality Check – Chernobyl and other fall-out areas
We propose to do a comparative analysis of the radioactivity numbers – and analyse the risks of living with low-dose radiation indefinitely.
There is an impressive body of scientific research on the effects of radiation on various population – in particular relating to the 26 largest nuclear accidents or events, starting with Nagasaki in 1945.
To make it real, we propose traveling to Chernobyl in Central Ukraine near the border with Belarus.
This year in April happens to be be the 30-year anniversary of the largest nuclear meltdown in the history of nuclear power generation – one of the reactors exploded during a routine test and the accident released extremely dangerous amounts of radioactive chemicals into the air, which over time contaminated millions of square miles in dozens of European nations.
It is estimated that thousands of deaths were directly caused by the explosion, while still more people suffered from illnesses brought about by radiation exposure.
The town closest to the No. 4 reactor was Pripyat, a city of 49,000 founded in 1970 to house workers from Chernobyl. Only about three kilometers from the plant, the entire city was forced to evacuate. Over two decades later, this ghost town is a freeze-frame of the Soviet Union in 1986.
It was opened as a tourist destination in 2002. To tour Pripyat, Chernobyl, and the surrounding villages, one must first obtain a day or several-day pass from the government. These passes can be obtained through the touring. There are five well-known tour agencies that take visitors to Pripyat.
High radiation levels forced the evacuation of more than 100,000 people from the region surrounding Chernobyl, but although about 700 residents have since returned to live in the region, none have reoccupied the actual town of Pripyat.
Almost thirty years after the accident, debate still rages about the number of directly related deaths. Fearing bad PR, the U.S.S.R. for several years forbade medical examiners from listing radiation as a cause of death. Estimates of deaths related to the accident range from 56 to thousands. The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests the final figure could reach 4,000 civilian deaths, a figure not including casualties amongst clean-up workers drawn from the Soviet military forces. The numbers presented for consequential death from radiation exposure induced illness and cancer vary considerably and range upward toward just short of 1,000,000 potential casualties. A Russian publication concluded that between 1986-2004 there were 985,000 premature cancer deaths worldwide as a result of radioactive contamination from Chernobyl.


Extra Budget Items:
Visit to Chernobyl -- approx R15,000 per person, crew of 3.
Or buy footage of "Most Radioactive place on Earth" -- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TRL7o2kPqw0

Press Release:


Nuclear Fallout
Could hair samples hold the answer to devastating illnesses plaguing hundreds of Johannesburg residents? A ground-breaking study is underway to investigate the extent to which uranium-rich waste, left over from 130 years of gold mining, is a health hazard for residents exposed to dust and contaminated water. Could this study bring hope to millions unwittingly living near radioactive waste on the Witwatersrand? Carte Blanche investigates.



PROMOS
 
TEN
What do mine dumps, uranium and hair stylists have in common? A ground-breaking international scientific study to see if Joburg residents are affected by dust from a hundred years of mining.
 
FIFTEEN
A world first – a World Health Organisation study into gold mining’s toxic inheritance: Is uranium-rich waste linked to cancer?
PROF FRANK WINDE: it hasn’t been done internationally on a large scale…up to 2.5 million people may be affected.
 
FIFTEEN
Can low level radiation from uranium-rich mine waste be linked to a rise in cancer?
ELANA COREEJES: You can see the beetroot, the lettuce leaves, with that dust blowing, if there’s uranium in it, we could be ingesting it, which could be the cause of all the stomach and colon cancers. 
 

Script:


NUCLEAR HAIR SCRIPT
A number of Johannesburg’s hairdressers have in recent months taken up scissors to snip their way into the world’s history books.
SHARYN GOLDMAN, HAIRLUSIONS: They were also very excited to be involved in a study that’s gonna actually help humanity. You get so few opportunities to do that and it’s an unconditional thing.
SEEISO SELEPE, DREADS OF CLASS: I feel good about the project, because I feel that people’s lives are being taken in to consideration…it’s going to save people’s lives.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Having a haircut is a routine event but some residents along the Witwatersrand are making a massive contribution to possibly solving a century old question.
Geography Prof Frank Winde from Northwest University has researched this question for thirty years: How does uranium affect people?
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: So uranium excites you?
PROF FRANK WINDE: It was a big problem in East Germany where I’m coming from, so I wanted to understand where must you intercept if you don’t want the people exposed to a toxic metal – the more knowledge you amass, the more interest.
Few scientists are closer to uranium than Winde – with two PhDs and an array of peer-reviewed international publications, he has now combined hundreds of scientific studies into one googlemap that shows how uranium gets into Johannesburg’s water, soil and air – from where it could affect residents.
Alongside Joburg homes, Winde’s map shows yellow mine dumps – whether they’re vegetated; how water runs across them to wash dust into into rivers. It even shows how far uranium particles travel in dust plumes.
PROF FRANK WINDE SCROLLING MAP: You see that the Fleurhof sides are safe but large parts in fact of Soweto are covered by dust and quite significantly and wherever you have overlapping dust problem exposure would be particular high.
FRANK WINDE: Up to 2.5 million people may be affected by that phenomenon.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Mine dumps are a common sight on the Witwatersrand – they’re also known as tailings dams…it’s estimated that there’s about 600-thousand tons of uranium in them.
Despite popular assumptions, it is not known to what degree ingested uranium is taken up by the body, but as long as hair is natural or untreated, the hair shaft is the simplest place to check, says stylist Sharyn Goldman.
SHARYN GOLDMAN: Hair keeps a tally of what your body’s been through like rings on a tree. As long as something’s been through your body, the blood supply will send it through to the hair and the hair will have a ring of that, so antibiotics, drugs, anaesthetic, anything anything shows up in your hair.
Microbiologist-turned-farmer Elana Coreejes drove by these prime vegetable farms in January and filmed the dust rising off a tailings dam on her cell phone. She had already noticed the unusually high incidence of cancer on her church’s prayer support list and decided to investigate.
ELANA COREEJES, FARMER: If you’re looking at the people’s treatment you see its kidney cancers, starting off with that. Thyroid cancers, liver cancers. Colon cancers, which brings us to the agriculture which is so intense in this specific area…you can see the beetroot, the lettuce leaves, with that dust blowing, if there’s uranium in it, we could be ingesting it, which could be the cause of all the stomach and colon cancers. 
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Why is uranium dangerous?
PROF FRANK WINDE: It’s actually the heaviest element which we find naturally earth and such it is a heavy metal and all heavy metals in a body usually have something called chemo-toxic properties. So it interferes with the working of liver or other cleaning organs and that is also true to uranium. It is also a radioactive metal so it kind of decays naturally.
Uranium occurs naturally at low concentrations everywhere on earth. In Johannesburg, it was brought from several thousand metres underground, as a byproduct of gold ore, for hundred and thirty years. Exposed to oxygen and water like this, it is released into the environment in high concentrations.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: This Bekkersdal – a township on the Far West Rand. Sixteen years ago Cecilia Mollo lost her sister from skin cancer. A year later her mom passed away from leukaemia and then just three years ago her dad was diagnosed with cancer of the prostate.
CECILIA LOOKING AT FAMILY PHOTOS: You can see the mine dumps right there.
CECILIA MOLLO, GENESIS FOUNDATION: In my mind it was possibly genetic, but when I checked in my neighborhood I had ten people in the same street.
DEVI: On the same street here?
CECILIA: Yes, I started doing research on word of mouth, it was beyond genetics, beyond coincidence. I suspect and I know in the core of my being that something is wrong in the environment, whether someone wants to admit is or not.
Using her own funds Cecilia now coordinates volunteers for home-based care and promotes cancer awareness. It began after she attended a presentation on the effects of mining by environmental justice campaigner Mariette Liefferink.
MARIETTE LIEFFERINK: Uranium is low in radioactivity; it has an extremely long half life. The shorter the half life, the higher the radioactivity, but uranium has very significant radioactive daughter, decay products. Such as RADIUM 226, THORIUM, BISHMUTH, POLONIUM, STRONTIUM and so forth. And also three lead isotopes that are radioactive. There is also of course radon – from RADIUM 226 you have radon gas.
CECILIA MOLLO: The Cooke section that we’re close to it is highly concentrated in Radium 226 and it causes cancer. It hit me at that point – is it possible that this might be the issue that is happening in this township? I started to ask questions. At the end of three months I had over a hundred people that had cancer.
While the link between radon and lung cancer is well established, uranium has not yet been proven to be cancer-causing, so in light of a weak world uranium price, there seems little impetus to enforce uranium clean-up – it only happens in cases where a good gold price makes reworking the last tailings profitable…like at Blyvoor, where a torrid three-year liquidation meant dewatered, collapsing dumps. Now new owners, Randlord Mines, face a community livid about the extreme dust, says director Richard Floyd.
RICHARD FLOYD. DIRECTOR, RANDLORD MINING: The gold price has increased by about 30% this year alone. There’s an investment to look for projects that will offer a good return…with the current gold price…just getting operational will address a majority of those challenges.
The law compels owners to rehabilitate as they mine and make radioactive land safe but with Mintails in business rescue consultant Anthony Turton says investment in radiologically toxic hotspots is key for the company to make it.
ANTHONY TURTON, MINTAILS CONSULTANT: The strategy is to remove those tailings dams over the next 3 years, to take it back to bare ground and then to start rehabilitating through grassing trials, etcetera. If you don’t attract capital into brown field sites the logical conclusion is that marginal companies will become insolvent that they simply walk away and all that happens under those circumstances is that the liability accrues to the state.
Sibanye Gold owns sixty percent of the one point three billion tons of tailings on the West Rand. Grant Stuart has to get all mines on board for a mammoth tailings dam by 2020 – a post-mining landscape with just one yellow dot.
GRANT STUART, SIBANYE INVESTOR RELATIONS: One thousand three hundred and fifty hectares are being set aside for all the tailings material from the entire area. If we are to put forward a solution that is environmentally friendly and socially responsible it would have to incorporate the whole of the West Rand that’s why you will see when we talk about a regional deposition storage facility or the final resting place for this tailings material it would have taken out the uranium, it would have taken out a large portion of the sulphur – it would be deposited into a modern facility that’s aligned with all the regulatory permitting requirements.
Cancer prevalence, Winde’s mapping of the pathways by which uranium could get into people’s bodies – like inhaling dust or ingesting water – and activism on international platforms finally caught the attention of the International Agency for Research on Cancer – an organ of the World Health Organisation. Epidemiologist Joachim Schuz heads the radiation and environment section.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: You wouldn’t just rush in unless you are concerned?
DR JOACHIM SCHUZ, INTERNATIONAL AGENCY FOR RESEARCH ON CANCER: We are driven by situations where we know we have open questions about cancer and environmental levels of uranium, really a controversial topic in cancer causation because we know that uranium miners have a higher cancer risk but this is not necessarily due to their uranium exposure because they are also exposed at the same time to some well-known and established carcinogens like radon and perhaps also the mine dust. When there is a situation that you have these at the environmental levels you can really investigate these open question on cancer causation then it is our mandate to actually took in to this.
Activist Lukas Moloto assisted in convincing hairdressers like Seeiso to approach their clients.
LUKAS MOLOTO, FEDERATION FOR A SUSTAINABLE ENVIRONMENT: We are trying to demystify and move away from the falsehood that is connected to the whole idea that there is no connection.
SEEISO SELEPE: I grew up in this area but I was never aware with the mine, the effects of the mine in this area.
CECILIA MOLLO: If someone can have a breakthrough like Mariette did with the World Health Organisation – that’s a major breakthrough.
DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: I would’ve assumed there we would already have formed the link…we’ve never done that?
PROF FRANK WINDE: No, it hasn’t been done and it hasn’t been done internationally on a large scale either.
DR JOACHIM SCHUZ: Beyond this potential public health problem we are really addressing global scientific question of cancer.
MARIETTE LIEFFERINK: There can of course be consequences, damages against certain mining companies, as was the case with asbestosis and silicosis…and for that reason there was a need to establish whether there is a causal link between the anecdotal evidence…and mine waste.
Three independent laboratories in Germany, Israel and at the Northwest University will take about a month to analyse and compare hair samples from 1600 people from affected and unaffected areas of Johannesburg. Results should be released in a few months when the data have been processed.

The numbers presented for consequential death from radiation exposure induced illness and cancer vary considerably and range upward toward just short of 1,000,000 potential casualties. A Russian publication concluded that between 1986-2004 there were 985,000 premature cancer deaths worldwide as a result of radioactive contamination from Chernobyl. Insert Details Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Voice-over Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Camera: Ben van Niekerk Offline editor: Hannes van Vuuren Online editor: Hannes van Vuuren Audio final mix: Floris Brand Insert Insert TC in Insert TC out Insert Duration 00:00:00 00:10:00 00:10:00 Booked Footage Footage returned: No Footage Declaration I confirm that all footage agreements have been signed and submitted via Jotform: No Music Cue Sheet Music Title Type Track Number Duration Publisher Composer Record/CD Number FIFTH WHEEL Background 36 00:00:40 Extreme SOCIETY 037 SOLAR OPPOSITE Background 7 00:00:22 Extreme JAMES S LEVINE 30 ESTEEM MACHINE Background 22 00:00:25 Extreme DOODLEY/WESSON 37 THE BOTTOM LINE Background 32 00:01:13 Exteme MEL WESSON 37 CUT AND RUN Background 29 00:00:19 Extreme MEL WESSON 15 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 10 April 2016 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 21 April 2016 Press Release: Nuclear Fallout Could hair samples hold the answer to devastating illnesses plaguing hundreds of Johannesburg residents? A ground-breaking study is underway to investigate the extent to which uranium-rich waste, left over from 130 years of gold mining, is a health hazard for residents exposed to dust and contaminated water. Could this study bring hope to millions unwittingly living near radioactive waste on the Witwatersrand? Carte Blanche investigates. PROMOS TEN What do mine dumps, uranium and hair stylists have in common? A ground-breaking international scientific study to see if Joburg residents are affected by dust from a hundred years of mining. FIFTEEN A world first – a World Health Organisation study into gold mining’s toxic inheritance: Is uranium-rich waste linked to cancer? PROF FRANK WINDE: it hasn’t been done internationally on a large scale…up to 2.5 million people may be affected. FIFTEEN Can low level radiation from uranium-rich mine waste be linked to a rise in cancer? ELANA COREEJES: You can see the beetroot, the lettuce leaves, with that dust blowing, if there’s uranium in it, we could be ingesting it, which could be the cause of all the stomach and colon cancers. Script: NUCLEAR HAIR SCRIPT A number of Johannesburg’s hairdressers have in recent months taken up scissors to snip their way into the world’s history books. SHARYN GOLDMAN, HAIRLUSIONS: They were also very excited to be involved in a study that’s gonna actually help humanity. You get so few opportunities to do that and it’s an unconditional thing. SEEISO SELEPE, DREADS OF CLASS: I feel good about the project, because I feel that people’s lives are being taken in to consideration…it’s going to save people’s lives. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Having a haircut is a routine event but some residents along the Witwatersrand are making a massive contribution to possibly solving a century old question. Geography Prof Frank Winde from Northwest University has researched this question for thirty years: How does uranium affect people? DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: So uranium excites you? PROF FRANK WINDE: It was a big problem in East Germany where I’m coming from, so I wanted to understand where must you intercept if you don’t want the people exposed to a toxic metal – the more knowledge you amass, the more interest. Few scientists are closer to uranium than Winde – with two PhDs and an array of peer-reviewed international publications, he has now combined hundreds of scientific studies into one googlemap that shows how uranium gets into Johannesburg’s water, soil and air – from where it could affect residents. Alongside Joburg homes, Winde’s map shows yellow mine dumps – whether they’re vegetated; how water runs across them to wash dust into into rivers. It even shows how far uranium particles travel in dust plumes. PROF FRANK WINDE SCROLLING MAP: You see that the Fleurhof sides are safe but large parts in fact of Soweto are covered by dust and quite significantly and wherever you have overlapping dust problem exposure would be particular high. FRANK WINDE: Up to 2.5 million people may be affected by that phenomenon. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Mine dumps are a common sight on the Witwatersrand – they’re also known as tailings dams…it’s estimated that there’s about 600-thousand tons of uranium in them. Despite popular assumptions, it is not known to what degree ingested uranium is taken up by the body, but as long as hair is natural or untreated, the hair shaft is the simplest place to check, says stylist Sharyn Goldman. SHARYN GOLDMAN: Hair keeps a tally of what your body’s been through like rings on a tree. As long as something’s been through your body, the blood supply will send it through to the hair and the hair will have a ring of that, so antibiotics, drugs, anaesthetic, anything anything shows up in your hair. Microbiologist-turned-farmer Elana Coreejes drove by these prime vegetable farms in January and filmed the dust rising off a tailings dam on her cell phone. She had already noticed the unusually high incidence of cancer on her church’s prayer support list and decided to investigate. ELANA COREEJES, FARMER: If you’re looking at the people’s treatment you see its kidney cancers, starting off with that. Thyroid cancers, liver cancers. Colon cancers, which brings us to the agriculture which is so intense in this specific area…you can see the beetroot, the lettuce leaves, with that dust blowing, if there’s uranium in it, we could be ingesting it, which could be the cause of all the stomach and colon cancers. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: Why is uranium dangerous? PROF FRANK WINDE: It’s actually the heaviest element which we find naturally earth and such it is a heavy metal and all heavy metals in a body usually have something called chemo-toxic properties. So it interferes with the working of liver or other cleaning organs and that is also true to uranium. It is also a radioactive metal so it kind of decays naturally. Uranium occurs naturally at low concentrations everywhere on earth. In Johannesburg, it was brought from several thousand metres underground, as a byproduct of gold ore, for hundred and thirty years. Exposed to oxygen and water like this, it is released into the environment in high concentrations. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: This Bekkersdal – a township on the Far West Rand. Sixteen years ago Cecilia Mollo lost her sister from skin cancer. A year later her mom passed away from leukaemia and then just three years ago her dad was diagnosed with cancer of the prostate. CECILIA LOOKING AT FAMILY PHOTOS: You can see the mine dumps right there. CECILIA MOLLO, GENESIS FOUNDATION: In my mind it was possibly genetic, but when I checked in my neighborhood I had ten people in the same street. DEVI: On the same street here? CECILIA: Yes, I started doing research on word of mouth, it was beyond genetics, beyond coincidence. I suspect and I know in the core of my being that something is wrong in the environment, whether someone wants to admit is or not. Using her own funds Cecilia now coordinates volunteers for home-based care and promotes cancer awareness. It began after she attended a presentation on the effects of mining by environmental justice campaigner Mariette Liefferink. MARIETTE LIEFFERINK: Uranium is low in radioactivity; it has an extremely long half life. The shorter the half life, the higher the radioactivity, but uranium has very significant radioactive daughter, decay products. Such as RADIUM 226, THORIUM, BISHMUTH, POLONIUM, STRONTIUM and so forth. And also three lead isotopes that are radioactive. There is also of course radon – from RADIUM 226 you have radon gas. CECILIA MOLLO: The Cooke section that we’re close to it is highly concentrated in Radium 226 and it causes cancer. It hit me at that point – is it possible that this might be the issue that is happening in this township? I started to ask questions. At the end of three months I had over a hundred people that had cancer. While the link between radon and lung cancer is well established, uranium has not yet been proven to be cancer-causing, so in light of a weak world uranium price, there seems little impetus to enforce uranium clean-up – it only happens in cases where a good gold price makes reworking the last tailings profitable…like at Blyvoor, where a torrid three-year liquidation meant dewatered, collapsing dumps. Now new owners, Randlord Mines, face a community livid about the extreme dust, says director Richard Floyd. RICHARD FLOYD. DIRECTOR, RANDLORD MINING: The gold price has increased by about 30% this year alone. There’s an investment to look for projects that will offer a good return…with the current gold price…just getting operational will address a majority of those challenges. The law compels owners to rehabilitate as they mine and make radioactive land safe but with Mintails in business rescue consultant Anthony Turton says investment in radiologically toxic hotspots is key for the company to make it. ANTHONY TURTON, MINTAILS CONSULTANT: The strategy is to remove those tailings dams over the next 3 years, to take it back to bare ground and then to start rehabilitating through grassing trials, etcetera. If you don’t attract capital into brown field sites the logical conclusion is that marginal companies will become insolvent that they simply walk away and all that happens under those circumstances is that the liability accrues to the state. Sibanye Gold owns sixty percent of the one point three billion tons of tailings on the West Rand. Grant Stuart has to get all mines on board for a mammoth tailings dam by 2020 – a post-mining landscape with just one yellow dot. GRANT STUART, SIBANYE INVESTOR RELATIONS: One thousand three hundred and fifty hectares are being set aside for all the tailings material from the entire area. If we are to put forward a solution that is environmentally friendly and socially responsible it would have to incorporate the whole of the West Rand that’s why you will see when we talk about a regional deposition storage facility or the final resting place for this tailings material it would have taken out the uranium, it would have taken out a large portion of the sulphur – it would be deposited into a modern facility that’s aligned with all the regulatory permitting requirements. Cancer prevalence, Winde’s mapping of the pathways by which uranium could get into people’s bodies – like inhaling dust or ingesting water – and activism on international platforms finally caught the attention of the International Agency for Research on Cancer – an organ of the World Health Organisation. Epidemiologist Joachim Schuz heads the radiation and environment section. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: You wouldn’t just rush in unless you are concerned? DR JOACHIM SCHUZ, INTERNATIONAL AGENCY FOR RESEARCH ON CANCER: We are driven by situations where we know we have open questions about cancer and environmental levels of uranium, really a controversial topic in cancer causation because we know that uranium miners have a higher cancer risk but this is not necessarily due to their uranium exposure because they are also exposed at the same time to some well-known and established carcinogens like radon and perhaps also the mine dust. When there is a situation that you have these at the environmental levels you can really investigate these open question on cancer causation then it is our mandate to actually took in to this. Activist Lukas Moloto assisted in convincing hairdressers like Seeiso to approach their clients. LUKAS MOLOTO, FEDERATION FOR A SUSTAINABLE ENVIRONMENT: We are trying to demystify and move away from the falsehood that is connected to the whole idea that there is no connection. SEEISO SELEPE: I grew up in this area but I was never aware with the mine, the effects of the mine in this area. CECILIA MOLLO: If someone can have a breakthrough like Mariette did with the World Health Organisation – that’s a major breakthrough. DEVI SANKAREE-GOVENDER: I would’ve assumed there we would already have formed the link…we’ve never done that? PROF FRANK WINDE: No, it hasn’t been done and it hasn’t been done internationally on a large scale either. DR JOACHIM SCHUZ: Beyond this potential public health problem we are really addressing global scientific question of cancer. MARIETTE LIEFFERINK: There can of course be consequences, damages against certain mining companies, as was the case with asbestosis and silicosis…and for that reason there was a need to establish whether there is a causal link between the anecdotal evidence…and mine waste. Three independent laboratories in Germany, Israel and at the Northwest University will take about a month to analyse and compare hair samples from 1600 people from affected and unaffected areas of Johannesburg. Results should be released in a few months when the data have been processed.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Hope for millions of people living in radioactive waste on the Witwatersrand gold fields - science steps in to bring their health plight to light
metadata.Summary: Hair tells a story, just like the rings on a tree or the circles on a turtle’s shell. Hair keeps everything that is put into the body – medication, drugs…and in a new study commissioned by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, an agency of the World Health Organisation, the hope is that for the first time hair will confirm the story, backed by science, that anecdotes of mental retardation, cancer and kidney disease have hinted at – namely that the uraniferous mine residue in the Witwatersrand Gold Fields can kill. And that urgent intervention is needed to save lives. In eight mining areas of the West Rand, the WHO has, after decades of tireless campaigning and activism, contracted the Federation for a Sustainable Environment to conduct a ground-breaking study to determine the effects of exposure to radio-active uranium-rich mine waste in the area. The Witwatersrand has 20 times more uranium dumps than the United States and Canada combined. More than 600 abandoned mines surround Joburg, with much of their waste now piled up high next to an estimated 1,6-million people – most of whom are poor and black and up to now powerless to take the fight in any direction because of a lack of solid science and an abundance of denial both form organized mining and the state. Mariette Liefferink from the FSE will now collect hair samples form cooperating hair salons near the waste dumps and send it off to three laboratories in three different countries, together with hair samples from salons further away from dumps – like in Alexandra, Randburg, Laudium and Lenasia. The FSE is conducting this research under supervision of the Northern West University.
metadata.Further information: The New Nuclear Backdrop President Jacob Zuma’s remarks during last week’s SONA on the country’s nuclear future might seem contradictory, but this is not the case, according to the organized nuclear industry. Zuma actually meant that South Africa’s nuclear build programme would roll out at a pace the country can afford and that the plan was to introduce 9600MW of nuclear energy in the next decade, they insist. Nuke lobbyists have been at pains to contain popular sentiment and to emphasise that the process of nuclear procurement has been extremely open and transparent – vendor parades were well documented within the confidentiality constraints of a competitive bidding process. Government has cancelled an unaffordable tender process in 2009 indicating the commitment to affordability. Basically, according to the pro-nuclear lobby, South Africa remains committed to 9600MW of Nuclear New Build, but we will do it at a scale and pace the country can afford and nuclear power remains by far the safest option What the nuclear industry fails to be transparent about is how much the mining of uranium will be upscaled to meet the demand of a new reactor. Whether environmental and health risks would even be considered. Science to the Rescue There seems to be an epidemic of cancer besetting the mining areas. Neighborhoods like Bekkersdal, sandwiched in between tailings dams and active mines, where virtually everyone in vivacious, energetic Cecilia Mollo’s street has cancer or know of someone who has fought or died of cancer. Thanks to the efforts of this former traffic official turned cancer activist, there is even more hope that science will bring to light an issue shrouded in mystery and denial from big mines, the uranium industry and even government. Cecilia lost her mother to melanoma, and her 19-year old sister to leukaemia. More recently she helped her 73-year old father battle prostate cancer. These experiences have opened the door to people taking Cecilia into their confidence about the great taboo of cancer – apart from believing it’s a white person’s disease, the prevalence just is not as high in other communities as it is here, around the mines. There’s also a wholesale ignorance of the contents of the uranium rich mine dumps in this area where pregnant women even collect the sand from the tailings, make mud and dry it into little cakes that they sell for as little as R5,00 a bag. The soil is bitten off or sucked and apparently satisfies hunger pangs and pregnancy cravings and tastes something like white chocolate. Except for the dire danger inherent in directly ingesting radio-active waste. Cecilia founded her own NGO to raise the issue, provide support – form getting money for people to get transport to hospitals in Johannesburg or Soweto, Baragwanath – over 60km away, since there are no oncology clinics in the area. Her own experiences with cancer and her steadfast outreach into the community had helped Cecilia collect anecdotes all over the township, and allowed her to present her preliminary findings both to the powerful Treatment Action Campaign as well as the internationally respected Medecins Sans Frontiers. The TAC assigned the soft-spoken Tsepho Maboe to help Cecilia conduct a door-to-door mapping of the Bekkersdal community to determine the extent of the prevalence of cancer. In no time Maboe has turned his extensive understanding of HIV and how to care for people into a deepening understanding of cancer. Once Cecilia and Tsepho have done the mapping, they have the promise from MSF that the research will form the basis of the first epidemiological study of cancer in the West Rand; and the Legal Resources Centre have suggested that the narratives be used as the basis for affidavits for a class action lawsuit. The people who live in the area we will show are all exposed to the uranium and other highly radioactive elements that come from the tailings dams in the catchment of the Upper Wonderfontein Spruit. In this catchment is the Lancaster Dam and an informal settlement on a nuclear dump that are said to be in the same order of radioactivity as the fall-out zone around Chernobyl. Reality Check – Chernobyl and other fall-out areas We propose to do a comparative analysis of the radioactivity numbers – and analyse the risks of living with low-dose radiation indefinitely. There is an impressive body of scientific research on the effects of radiation on various population – in particular relating to the 26 largest nuclear accidents or events, starting with Nagasaki in 1945. To make it real, we propose traveling to Chernobyl in Central Ukraine near the border with Belarus. This year in April happens to be be the 30-year anniversary of the largest nuclear meltdown in the history of nuclear power generation – one of the reactors exploded during a routine test and the accident released extremely dangerous amounts of radioactive chemicals into the air, which over time contaminated millions of square miles in dozens of European nations. It is estimated that thousands of deaths were directly caused by the explosion, while still more people suffered from illnesses brought about by radiation exposure. The town closest to the No. 4 reactor was Pripyat, a city of 49,000 founded in 1970 to house workers from Chernobyl. Only about three kilometers from the plant, the entire city was forced to evacuate. Over two decades later, this ghost town is a freeze-frame of the Soviet Union in 1986. It was opened as a tourist destination in 2002. To tour Pripyat, Chernobyl, and the surrounding villages, one must first obtain a day or several-day pass from the government. These passes can be obtained through the touring. There are five well-known tour agencies that take visitors to Pripyat. High radiation levels forced the evacuation of more than 100,000 people from the region surrounding Chernobyl, but although about 700 residents have since returned to live in the region, none have reoccupied the actual town of Pripyat. Almost thirty years after the accident, debate still rages about the number of directly related deaths. Fearing bad PR, the U.S.S.R. for several years forbade medical examiners from listing radiation as a cause of death. Estimates of deaths related to the accident range from 56 to thousands. The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests the final figure could reach 4,000 civilian deaths, a figure not including casualties amongst clean-up workers drawn from the Soviet military forces. The numbers presented for consequential death from radiation exposure induced illness and cancer vary considerably and range upward toward just short of 1,000,000 potential casualties. A Russian publication concluded that between 1986-2004 there were 985,000 premature cancer deaths worldwide as a result of radioactive contamination from Chernobyl.
